name: Diana Harshbarger
bio: Two-term incumbent first elected 2020. Trump-endorsed; expected to win re-nomination handily.
photo_credit: U.S. House Office of the Clerk

early_childhood_ed.summary: No publicly stated position found on federal early childhood programs such as Head Start; continues to support school choice and state/local control over education.
early_childhood_ed.details: No new statements or votes by Rep. Harshbarger specifically addressing early childhood education programs were found in the June 14–29, 2026 window or the July 1–6, 2026 window. Her longstanding position favors school choice and state and local control over education policy. On June 26, 2026, she introduced the Nutrition Education and Chronic Disease Prevention in Community Health Centers Act of 2026, which would fund nutrition education and counseling at federally qualified health centers, with priority given to communities with high rates of food insecurity and diet-related chronic disease — a measure with indirect benefits for children's health. No co-sponsorships of Head Start funding legislation or publicly stated positions on federal pre-K programs have been identified.

child_hunger.summary: Introduced nutrition education legislation in June 2026; previously voted for SNAP restrictions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and the Nutritious SNAP Act. As of June 2026, approximately 100,000 Tennesseans have lost SNAP benefits since the law took effect. A federal court blocked Tennessee's planned SNAP food restrictions (Healthy SNAP Tennessee) on June 22, 2026.
child_hunger.details: On June 26, 2026, Rep. Harshbarger introduced the Nutrition Education and Chronic Disease Prevention in Community Health Centers Act of 2026, which would authorize HRSA to fund evidence-based nutrition education and counseling at community health centers, with priority for communities with high food insecurity. The bill aligns with the 'Make America Healthy Again' agenda she cited. Separately, Harshbarger's prior votes include support for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and the Nutritious SNAP Act of 2025, which restricted SNAP-eligible foods and tightened eligibility. As of June 2026, approximately 100,000 Tennesseans have lost SNAP benefits since the law's July 2025 effective date, according to Tennessee Lookout reporting. In the July 1–6, 2026 window, a federal court ruling on June 22, 2026 (Aragon v. Rollins) voided USDA-approved waivers that would have allowed Tennessee to restrict SNAP benefits from covering soda and sugary processed foods (the Healthy SNAP Tennessee initiative, planned to take effect July 31). U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson held that USDA Secretary Rollins lacked statutory authority to redefine eligible food through waivers. No new votes or statements from Harshbarger specifically responding to this ruling were found in the July 1–6 window.

parental_support.summary: On July 2, 2026, Harshbarger published an op-ed championing the Working Families Tax Cuts, highlighting the launch of Trump Accounts — new tax-deferred savings accounts for children under age 18 that opened July 4, 2026. Prior record includes co-sponsoring the Parents Bill of Rights Act and voting for the expanded Child Tax Credit.
parental_support.details: On July 2, 2026, Rep. Harshbarger published an op-ed in the Elizabethton Star marking the one-year anniversary of the Working Families Tax Cuts. She noted the law delivered $82 billion in individual tax relief in its first year (97% of filers received a cut; nearly 70% earned under $100,000). In the column, she specifically highlighted the July 4, 2026 launch of Trump Accounts — tax-deferred savings accounts created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act for children under the age of 18, designed to grow through investment earnings and give children a financial head start into adulthood. She also cited No Tax on Tips and No Tax on Overtime provisions as benefiting working families across East Tennessee. Her existing record includes a YES vote on the Tax Relief for American Families and Workers Act (HR 7024, Jan. 2024), which expanded the Child Tax Credit, and co-sponsorship of the Parents Bill of Rights Act. The nutrition education bill she introduced in late June 2026 has indirect relevance to family health outcomes but is not a parental-support measure per se.

name: Tim Burchett
bio: Three-term incumbent serving since 2019. Outspoken populist conservative; minimal primary opposition.
photo_credit: U.S. House Office of the Clerk

early_childhood_ed.summary: No publicly stated position supporting federal early childhood education programs; no new statements found in the June 14–29, 2026 or July 1–6, 2026 windows.
early_childhood_ed.details: No new statements, legislation, or votes from Rep. Tim Burchett specifically addressing early childhood education or federal childcare programs were found in the June 14–29, 2026 or July 1–6, 2026 search windows. His public activities in these periods focused heavily on SNAP fraud oversight and related legislation, and on birthright citizenship. His voting record continues to show a low rate of support for tracked education bills (26% support / 74% oppose). No co-sponsorships of Head Start funding or pre-K legislation have been identified.

child_hunger.summary: Chaired a June 25, 2026 House DOGE subcommittee hearing on SNAP fraud; introduced H.R.9456 on June 25, 2026 to restrict SNAP eligibility to lawful permanent residents with at least 10 years of U.S. residency; previously voted for SNAP cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. As of June 2026, approximately 100,000 Tennesseans have lost SNAP benefits since the law took effect. A federal court blocked Tennessee's planned SNAP food restrictions on June 22, 2026.
child_hunger.details: On June 19, 2026, Rep. Burchett, as chairman of the House Subcommittee on Delivering on Government Efficiency (DOGE), announced a hearing titled 'Combating Waste, Fraud, and Abuse in SNAP,' held June 25, 2026. At the hearing, he announced plans to introduce bills targeting SNAP fraud; one of these bills was introduced that same day as H.R.9456 (119th Congress), which would amend the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008 to restrict SNAP eligibility for non-citizens to those admitted as lawful permanent residents who have resided in the United States for at least 10 years. H.R.9456 was referred to the House Agriculture Committee on June 25, 2026, with no cosponsors. Burchett also sent letters to five Democratic governors demanding SNAP beneficiary data and cited $10 billion in improper SNAP payments in 2024 and USDA identification of $3 billion in potential fraud. Context: A June 16, 2026 Tennessee Lookout report documented that approximately 100,000 Tennesseans lost SNAP benefits since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Burchett previously supported, took effect in July 2025. Additionally, on June 22, 2026, a federal court (Aragon v. Rollins) voided USDA-approved waivers that would have allowed Tennessee to restrict SNAP purchases of sugary foods and beverages under the Healthy SNAP Tennessee initiative, which had been set to take effect July 31. No public statement from Burchett in response to this court ruling was found in the July 1–6, 2026 window.

parental_support.summary: Voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which raised the Child Tax Credit to $2,200 per child and expanded the employer childcare credit; in July 2026, expressed disappointment with the Supreme Court's ruling upholding birthright citizenship and called on Congress to act; no new parental-support legislation found in the June 14–29 or July 1–6, 2026 windows.
parental_support.details: Burchett's most significant parental-support action remains his vote for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which increased the Child Tax Credit from $2,000 to $2,200 per child and expanded the employer childcare tax credit. In July 2026, Burchett publicly expressed disappointment with the Supreme Court's June 30, 2026 ruling that reaffirmed birthright citizenship under the Fourteenth Amendment (Trump v. Barbara), and joined other Tennessee Republicans in calling on Congress to take legislative action on the issue. His position aligns with the broader Republican effort to restrict birthright citizenship through legislation, though the court's ruling suggests a constitutional amendment would be required for a fundamental change. No new legislation or public statements from Burchett specifically addressing paid family leave, childcare costs, or child tax policy were found in the June 14–29, 2026 or July 1–6, 2026 search windows. His June 2026 public activities centered on SNAP oversight and a ribbon-cutting at the McNabb Center's new mental health transition campus in Blount County.

Fleischmann chairs the House Energy and Water Development Appropriations Subcommittee; his July 2026 public presence remains concentrated on energy and federal science funding rather than education policy. His long-standing record favors returning education decisions to states and local communities, opposing federal standards and funding expansions for early childhood programs. Fleischmann voted in favor of the One Big Beautiful Bill. He also voted against the American Rescue Plan’s expanded child nutrition provisions. A federal court on June 22, 2026 voided Tennessee’s planned Healthy SNAP Tennessee restrictions (widely reported July 1–2), which would have barred SNAP recipients from purchasing sugary foods starting July 31; Fleischmann made no public statement on the ruling in the July 1–6 window. A July 3 Chattanooga Times Free Press “Rants” column criticized Fleischmann for failing to secure Oak Ridge funding but contained no new child hunger policy statements. No new statements from Fleischmann specifically addressing child hunger or food assistance programs were found in the July 1–6 window. parental_support.summary: Supported the 2017 child tax credit expansion and the One Big Beautiful Bill's tax provisions; voted against the 2021 expanded Child Tax Credit; champions parental rights in school settings.
parental_support.details: Fleischmann supported the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act expansion of the Child Tax Credit to $2,000 per child and voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill, which makes the baseline $2,000 CTC permanent. His public record emphasizes parental rights in educational settings, including opposition to federal curriculum mandates. As Energy and Water Appropriations chair, his early July 2026 public statements focused on federal science and energy funding, not family policy.

Andy Ogles through July 6, 2026. Ogles has previously opposed federal education spending increases and supported school choice and arming teachers. The DCCC has documented approximately $10 million in federal education grants withheld from his district. His July 2026 legislative activity focused on immigration policy (the Anchors Away Act, introduced June 30) rather than education. child_hunger.details: Rep. Ogles' voting record on child hunger remains defined by his yes vote on the One Big Beautiful Bill (H.R. 1, 2025), which included approximately $200 billion in SNAP cuts. A June 16, 2026 Tennessee Lookout report documented that nearly 100,000 Tennesseans have lost SNAP benefits since the bill took effect in July 2025. Ogles' August 2025 social media post — 'MAHA! If you want to be healthy, don't eat junk food' — drew attention in this context. On June 22, 2026, a federal judge voided Tennessee's SNAP waiver that would have restricted purchases of soda and sugary processed foods under the 'Healthy SNAP Tennessee' initiative (which had been set to begin July 31, 2026), ruling that the USDA lacked statutory authority to approve such waivers. Ogles made no public comment on this ruling as of July 6, 2026. No new statements from Ogles specifically addressing child hunger, SNAP, or school meals were found in July 1–6, 2026 coverage.

parental_support.summary: New July 2026 activity: After the Supreme Court upheld birthright citizenship (Trump v. Barbara, 6-3, June 30, 2026), Ogles introduced the 'Anchors Away Act' on June 30/July 1, banning pregnant noncitizens from entering the U.S. and requiring U.S.-born children of parents who lose citizenship to be deported with them. Combined with his June 25 Remigration Act and earlier deleted 'homosexuality has no place in America' post, Ogles' July 2026 legislative activity reflects sharp anti-immigration positions with direct consequences for immigrant families and children. Previously voted yes on the One Big Beautiful Bill which extended the $2,000 CTC.
parental_support.details: On June 30, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Barbara to uphold birthright citizenship, striking down an executive order by President Trump. Hours later, Rep. Ogles introduced the 'Anchors Away Act,' which would: (1) restrict birthright citizenship so that a child born in the U.S. is only automatically a citizen if at least one parent is a U.S. citizen, green card holder, or lawfully present military member; (2) bar pregnant noncitizens from entering the U.S. on nonimmigrant visas unless married to a U.S. citizen (with a medical exception for childbirth treatment); and (3) require children to be deported with parents who lose citizenship, unless the other parent is a U.S. citizen who retains custody. Ogles appeared on Fox News, Newsmax, and Fox News Radio to promote the bill in the July 1–2 period, calling the SCOTUS ruling a 'betrayal of America.' This legislation directly affects immigrant families with U.S.-born children. On June 1, 2026, Ogles posted from his official account 'Homosexuality has no place in America. Happy Nuclear Family Month,' before deleting the message and blaming a staffer. On June 25, 2026, he introduced the Remigration Act, a discussion draft bill that would end birthright citizenship for children of undocumented immigrants born after enactment, revoke naturalized citizenship for certain convictions within 10 years, and create a DHS task force to review Biden-era asylum grants. Ogles previously voted yes on the One Big Beautiful Bill, which extended the $2,000 child tax credit, but voted against the 2024 bipartisan child tax credit expansion and has not supported paid family leave. His DOJ investigation ended in May 2026 when the DOJ agreed to return his phone and destroy seized evidence related to the children's burial garden campaign fundraising controversy.

name: Charlie Hatcher
bio: Endorsed by former Gov. Bill Haslam and former Sen. Bob Corker. Considered the strongest Republican challenger to Ogles. $546K in FEC receipts with $214K cash on hand (Q1 2026).
photo_credit: University of Tennessee Institute of Agriculture

early_childhood_ed.summary: New July 2026 statement: Hatcher cited high childcare costs as a family affordability crisis and called for education to return to 'the basics' of reading, writing, arithmetic, and civics, while emphasizing teacher pay. Campaign continues to focus on contrast with Ogles rather than specific federal early childhood education policy.
early_childhood_ed.details: During a Hickman County campaign visit reported July 2, 2026, Charlie Hatcher explicitly named childcare as a cost-of-living burden on Tennessee families, stating: 'The energy prices are high and gas prices. Childcare is high, groceries are high. The cost of living… For the average person, the American Dream is almost not attainable.' On public education, he stated: 'I think we need to get back to basics, in education, reading, writing, arithmetic, and civics. But we need to pay teachers well… They’re shaping kids’ lives.' These are his most substantive public comments on education to date. However, Hatcher has not articulated specific federal policy positions on early childhood education, pre-K funding, Head Start, or childcare investment programs. His framing remains cost-of-living and results-focused rather than specific policy proposals. He was confirmed as the speaker for the Henry County Farm Bureau's annual membership meeting on July 14, 2026. Former Rep. Zach Wamp previously endorsed Hatcher in the TN-5 GOP primary.

His July 2026 campaign appearances focused on his contrasting style with Ogles and his record of practical governance. He is scheduled to speak at the Henry County Farm Bureau on July 14, 2026.

parental_support.details: In a July 2, 2026 Hickman County campaign visit, Charlie Hatcher framed childcare affordability as a central threat to the American Dream for Tennessee families, alongside high energy, gas, and grocery costs. He is scheduled to speak at the Henry County Farm Bureau on July 14, 2026.
